reliability_summary: The Hyundai i20 (PB generation, 2012-2015) with the 1.4L 100hp engine and 4-speed torque-converter automatic is generally well regarded: the i20 line has repeatedly placed in the top 10 of What Car?'s reliability surveys and won Auto Bild's TÜV Report 2019 best-compact-car award with only 3% serious-defect rate. This specific combo uses a conventional planetary automatic (not the later dual-clutch robotic gearbox found in some Hyundai/Kia models), which avoids the DCT-related jerking/clutch-wear complaints seen in 2014-2016 models. The main known issue across 2012-2015 i20s is AC compressor failure/refrigerant leaks around 50,000-70,000km; some owners also report delayed or jerky shifts starting around 60,000-80,000km, fixable via fluid change or valve-body service. CarComplaints shows relatively few filed complaints for this generation, suggesting either low reported-issue volume or low sample size. Israeli sources describe the model as generally reliable but flag checking the cooling system for overheating risk. Confidence is medium: survey data is strong but mostly UK/German-market, and Israeli-specific long-term data on this exact engine/gearbox combo is thin. Sources: What Car? reliability surveys, Auto Bild TÜV Report 2019, CarComplaints.com, AUTODOC BLOG, motor-center.co.il, auto.co.il.

General reliability surveys put the Fiat 500 below segment average (JD Power ~70/100, RepairPal 18/21, US News 12/13 subcompacts), consistent with the gearbox complaints rather than contradicting them. Confidence is medium: the Dualogic identification is inferred from the model year/engine/market (not explicitly confirmed on this specific listing), and no Israel-specific forum threads on this exact combo were found, though general sources agree closely.

reliability_summary: Overall the Spark's 1.4L 4-speed automatic is a mid-pack, not a top-tier, choice: US complaint trackers list 2017 among the Spark's worse years for transmission gripes (delayed/rough 1-2 shifts, occasional shudder around 50-55mph), while the same sources note the 2016-2022 generation was notably quieter on serious defects than the rough 2013-2015 years. GM issued a free TCM reprogramming recall (N192268880) for 2016-2018 Sparks to fix a software issue where a faulty TCM memory bank could hide fault codes - a software fix, not a hardware failure, and low-cost/low-risk. Typical transmission repair costs cited for the Spark line run $1,500-3,000 in the rare failure cases, though only a handful of formal complaints exist for the 2017 model specifically. Israeli owner forums (CarsForum, FXP) show mixed but mostly unremarkable experiences, with some noting Korean-built GM small cars hold up well for roughly 5 years before wear issues accumulate. Evidence is thin/conflicting between 'worst years' lists and 'quieter generation' claims, so confidence is medium; sources: CarComplaints.com, KBB, RepairPal, NHTSA recall N192268880, carsforum.co.il, fxp.co.il.

reliability_summary: Toyota Auris Hybrid (2013-2019, 1.8L + eCVT) has a strong reliability record, topping the 2012 Which? survey at 96.4% and generally seen as one of the most dependable used hatchbacks. The eCVT hybrid transaxle itself is a planetary-gear design with no clutches/belts and routinely lasts 250,000-300,000+ km with basic maintenance, so the gearbox is not a concern. The main model-wide risks are the hybrid drive battery, which starts losing capacity around 150,000 km and can fail outright between 200,000-250,000 km, and an Intelligent Power Module recall affecting cars built May 2014-Dec 2018 (free dealer fix, worth confirming was done). This specific car is a 2014 build at 198,000 km, right inside the hybrid-battery risk window, so a dealer battery health check before purchase is warranted. Secondary issues noted across sources: AC compressor/pipe wear after 50-70k km, occasional CVT sensor glitches, and a cooling-pump weak point common to Toyota hybrids generally. Sources: Which? used-car reliability survey, Toyota Owners Club forum threads, autodoc.co.uk/driversadvice.com fault summaries, Israeli auto.co.il/icar.co.il/carguru.co.il listings and reviews.

reliability_summary: This generation Picanto (2011-2015) with the 1.2 Kappa engine and 4-speed torque-converter automatic is generally solid: the engine is chain-driven with no major recurring faults, and UK owner-satisfaction surveys rate the model well overall. The automatic gearbox (a conventional 4AT, not a problem-prone DCT) is the main known weak point, with owners reporting jerky/delayed shifts and solenoid or speed-sensor faults emerging from roughly 60,000-80,000km if fluid isn't changed every 40-60k km; at 149,000km this car is well past that threshold so the transmission should be tested carefully before purchase. A fuel-filler-neck hose recall covers Feb 2011-Jun 2012 builds (this car is on the edge of that range) and is a cheap fix if unresolved. Israeli owners have also flagged real-world fuel consumption on the automatic running higher than advertised (a 2013 class-action against the importer), which is a running-cost issue rather than a reliability one. Evidence is consistent across UK consumer sites, gearbox-repair specialists, and Israeli forums, but detailed Israeli long-term reliability data is thin, hence medium confidence. Sources: WhatCar/Carbuyer reliability reviews, ASR Gearbox Repairs, CarComplaints.com recalls, carsforum.co.il, thecar.co.il.

reliability_summary: Subaru as a brand rates well above average in reliability surveys, and the 1.6L FB16 naturally-aspirated engine has no major reported design flaws beyond being underpowered and occasional oil consumption. The weak point is the Lineartronic CVT: 2012-2017 XV/Crosstrek units are widely flagged (forums, CarsGuide, motorverso, Rohnert Park Transmission) for shudder, whine, delayed engagement and chain/valve-body wear, with many needing rebuild around 100,000-160,000km if fluid wasn't serviced early and often - and this specific car is already at 222,146km, well past that typical failure window, so realized risk is meaningfully higher than for a lower-mileage example. Israeli sources (auto.co.il, jeepolog forums) echo this: transmission is fine if well maintained but wears faster than competitors and isn't built for heavy loads. A few older XVs also had a recalled brake-light switch (pre-Sept 2016, likely not applicable at 2017 model) and early wheel-bearing/CV-joint wear. Evidence is consistent across English and Hebrew sources with no major conflicts, but confidence is medium because no source gives CVT longevity data specific to Israeli climate/driving or this exact mileage band. Sources: CarsGuide, What Car?, motorverso.com, Rohnert Park Transmission, SubaruXVForum, auto.co.il, jeepolog.com forums.

reliability_summary: This is the 1.6 GDI naturally-aspirated engine with a conventional torque-converter automatic (not the turbo/DCT combo), which multiple UK sources (Carbuyer, Autodoc, carchecker.pro) flag as the more reliable Sportage QL powertrain, commonly exceeding 200,000km with proper maintenance. Known issues for this combo are mild: GDI intake-valve carbon buildup (generic to direct-injection engines, manageable with periodic cleaning) and some owner reports of stiffer shifts or oil consumption at high mileage. A real concern is the HECU (hydraulic electronic control unit) fire recall covering 2017-2021 Sportage models, plus a separate tow-hitch wiring fire recall - worth confirming recall completion on this specific VIN. Israeli-language sources found were low-quality SEO content generically bashing Hyundai/Kia engines rather than this specific combo, so they were discounted. NHTSA logs 147 complaints for the 2018 model year, mostly tied to the trailer-hitch recall rather than engine/transmission failures. Net: above-average reliability for the model line, tempered by the recall history and reliance on non-Israeli sources - confidence medium. Sources: carbuyer.co.uk, autodoc.co.uk, carchecker.pro, nhtsa.gov, carcomplaints.com.

reliability_summary: This is a 2013 Hyundai i20 (PB gen) with the 1.4L Kappa petrol engine and a conventional 4-speed torque-converter automatic, not Hyundai's riskier dual-clutch/robotic gearbox, which avoids the worst-known Hyundai/Kia transmission failure mode. General model reliability is solid (CarReliabilityReport rates the PB-gen i20 7.6/10; petrol variants recommended over diesel), and Israeli listings/forums describe the model as generally dependable with only scattered owner complaints about electrics and trim quality. The 4-speed automatic itself has documented weak points across forums (Hyundai Forums, ASR Gearbox Repairs): jerky or delayed shifts and occasional slippage typically emerging around 60,000-80,000km, worse with heavy city/stop-and-go use - this car's 161,456km puts it well past that threshold, so a transmission service history and test-drive check for shift quality are important. No recalls or systemic design-flaw failures were found (unlike Hyundai/Kia DCT models). Confidence is medium: broad model reliability data is solid, but little Israel-specific or automatic-specific long-term data exists, and this generation's automatic reliability rests mainly on forum reports rather than structured surveys.

reliability_summary: Low reliability for this specific combo: the 2017 Altima's 2.5L Xtronic CVT has a well-documented design flaw (undersized/poor cooling causing fluid overheating, belt/pulley wear) that triggered multiple class-action lawsuits and a Nissan-issued extended powertrain warranty (84 months/84,000 miles) for 2012-2017 CVT vehicles. CarComplaints.com logs 32+ transmission complaints for this model year, including full transmission failures, jerking, hesitation, and limp-mode, with an average failure mileage around 56,000 miles (~90,000 km) - well below this listing's 193,000 km, meaning it is almost certainly past any warranty coverage and at high risk of needing a CVT replacement soon. Owner forums (NissanClub, Car Talk) corroborate the same symptoms independently of the lawsuit sources. No conflicting evidence found; sources consistently agree this is a known systemic fault, so per the rubric the score is capped at the low end regardless of brand reputation. Sources: CarComplaints.com, TopClassActions.com/ClassAction.org (Xtronic CVT class action coverage), NissanClub owner forum, Car Talk community forum.

reliability_summary: The naturally-aspirated 1.6 GDI (Gamma, 133hp) paired with the 6-speed automatic is generally regarded as one of the more solid Sportage QL powertrains, with no major engine design flaw reported (no timing-chain or block issues), and Israeli owner reports (car-pad.co.il, carzone.co.il) describe strong long-term reliability with low maintenance costs. The main known issue is GDI intake-valve carbon buildup common to direct-injection engines, plus occasional delayed/harsh automatic shifting reported by RepairPal in roughly 6% of 2015-2016 cars, typically surfacing 110,000-190,000km - a window this car (220,000km) has already passed without apparent issue per the listing. All 2015 Sportage QL units are subject to an NHTSA HECU (ABS module) fire-risk recall that should be verified as completed before purchase. Evidence is somewhat mixed: CarComplaints/Consumer Reports rate the 2015 model year below average overall, but those complaint counts aggregate all engines/trims (including turbo/diesel) rather than this specific 1.6 GDI+auto combo, which skews more positive in engine-specific sources. Given the thin, partly conflicting US-market data mixed with more favorable Israeli and engine-specific sources, confidence is medium. reliability_summary: Below-average reliability: this first-gen (2007-2016) Compass with the 2.0L/CVT automatic combo has a well-documented design flaw in its Jatco-based CVT, which owner forums (JeepGarage, MyJeepCompass, JeepPatriotForums) and transmission specialist sites consistently report as prone to overheating, jerking, slipping, and delayed engagement, with failures often needing a ~$3,500 replacement. Consumer Reports rated this generation Compass mediocre overall, though notably better than the related Patriot. A 2010-2014 NHTSA recall (airbag OCR module short-circuit risk) also applies to this model year, though that's a fixable safety recall, not a chronic wear issue. At 145,000km and hand 6, this specific car is well into the mileage range where CVT problems typically surface. Evidence is consistent across sources but mostly US-market (CVT variant confirmation for the Israeli 154hp spec is inferred, not directly verified), so confidence is medium rather than high.

reliability_summary: The 2014 Juke's 1.6 NA + Jatco CVT (Xtronic) combo has a well-documented design flaw, so score is capped despite decent general brand reputation. Multiple independent sources (Juke Owners Club, Juke Forums, RepairPal, transmission specialist sites) report jerky acceleration, shuddering, whining and outright CVT failure often before 50k-80k miles, usually traced to internal bearing wear and inadequate cooling under sustained highway load - directly relevant given Itay's twice-weekly highway trips. This is corroborated by Israeli sources: a documented class-action settlement covering ~10,000 Nissan Juke units in Israel with the same Jatco CVT defect, with Nissan/Jatco aware of the issue. Consumer Reports/JD Power/KBB owner surveys are more mixed, with ~80% of owners recommending the car, and a 2012-2014 recall exists for a separate fuel-pressure-sensor leak issue. Evidence is consistent and high-confidence on the CVT flaw itself; no data found on this specific unit's transmission service history, so an inspection/fluid-change record check is recommended before purchase.

reliability_summary: Below-average reliability for this specific combo: the LTG 2.0T engine (GM's Ecotec turbo used across Malibu/Regal/ATS) has a documented design flaw with sticking oil control rings and piston/carbon issues that cause oil burning and can require engine rebuild or replacement, well-corroborated across owner forums and repair write-ups. The 6-speed automatic paired with it also has a known valve body defect causing hesitation/shaking on acceleration, plus general complaints of failures, slipping and rough shifts (CarComplaints, Chevy Malibu Forums). Israeli sources describe the car as generally serviceable but call the gearbox's shift quality poor, and note the Malibu trails Toyota Camry-level reliability with higher upkeep costs. At this listing's 213,000km the car is well past the mileage range (80-150k km) where these engine/transmission issues typically surface, so risk is elevated versus a lower-mileage example. Evidence rests mainly on US enthusiast forums and CarComplaints rather than large-scale statistical surveys (no Consumer Reports data pulled for this trim), so confidence is medium. Sources: chevymalibuforum.com threads on 2.0T engine/valve-body failures, carcomplaints.com transmission page, 8020automotive Ecotec problems writeup, carsforum.co.il and fxp.co.il Hebrew owner threads.

reliability_summary: Renault Megane IV 1.5 dCi with EDC dual-clutch automatic gets mixed-to-average reliability marks: the diesel engine itself is broadly sound but the EDC gearbox is the recurring weak point, with jerky 1-2/3-4 shifts, 'Check Auto Gearbox' warnings, clutch actuator solenoid failures (~€300-500) and occasional full mechatronic unit replacement (~€1,200-2,000), especially in stop-start city driving. Multiple UK sources (Autocar, WhatCar, ASR Gearbox Repairs, automotive24) agree post-2019/2020 software updates reduced but didn't eliminate the shifting issues. The 1.5 dCi also has known turbo/injector/EGR wear and DPF clogging risk on short low-speed trips. This specific car has 283,000 km on the clock at only 1st hand and 2020 model year - far beyond the ~100,000 km point sources flag for checking EDC service history, so gearbox condition and service records here matter more than the general model rating. Evidence is decent (4+ independent automotive sources agree) but thin on Israeli-market-specific data for this exact engine/gearbox combo, hence medium confidence.

reliability_summary: Renault Fluence 1.5 dCi (110hp, EDC dual-clutch automatic) rates average: no catastrophic design flaw but several recurring weak points across independent sources. The dual-clutch automatic itself has scattered owner/dealer reports of gearbox-control-unit faults and 'Check Auto Gearbox' warnings, with clutch pack wear needing careful maintenance. The 1.5 dCi engine is known for DPF clogging on short urban trips, injector wear/failure sensitive to fuel quality (one forum owner at 250k km needed two injectors), and a 60,000km cambelt interval that must not be skipped. General Fluence complaints (CarComplaints) also flag A/C condenser leaks and minor recalls (wheel bolt torque, rear hub carrier). This specific car is already at 275,000km, well past where these wear items typically surface, so inspection of DPF/injectors/gearbox condition is important. Evidence is consistent across UK/EU forums, CarComplaints and an Israeli long-term test (Auto magazine) but is generic to the 1.5 dCi/EDC combo rather than this exact model year, hence medium confidence.

The 182hp automatic uses a 6-speed torque-converter gearbox, but Israeli owners filed a further class-action request alleging systemic automatic-transmission failure in the same 2015-2019 Kuga/Focus EcoBoost family. UK surveys (What Car?, Driver Power) rate the petrol Kuga close to average overall, with electrics (screen/camera lockups) and power-steering pump wear as other recurring complaints around 100k+ km. reliability_summary: The 2017 Malibu with the 1.5T/6-speed automatic is a below-average-reliability model year: Consumer Reports rates it worse than peers with 4 NHTSA recalls, and US owner forums/complaint sites report engine 'reduced power' warnings with knocking (sometimes from turbo or piston/compression issues) starting as low as 30,000 miles, plus cold-start stalling. The automatic transmission has a recurring 'shift to park' fault that can strand the car and hard/jerky shifting and slipping complaints. GM reportedly improved this powertrain from 2019-2020 on, so the 2016-2017 cars specifically carry the worst reputation. Israeli sources (auto.co.il, FXP, icar) are thinner and more mixed - some owners report zero issues, one forum flags the era's engine reliability as questionable - so local corroboration is weaker than the US data. This engine/transmission combo has a known design-flaw pattern for this model year, capping the score at moderate; with 190,000 km already on the clock (well past where issues start appearing), risk is elevated. Sources: Consumer Reports, CarComplaints-style aggregators, chevymalibuforum.com, auto.co.il, FXP forum.

reliability_summary: The 2018 Peugeot 5008 1.6 THP 165 with automatic (EAT6) gearbox has two specific known weak points that cap the score: the EAT6 automatic's mechatronic unit is a recognized failure point around 60,000-130,000km (harsh shifts, hesitation, occasional total loss of drive; repair ~£1,500-5,000), and the 1.6 THP engine is known for timing chain wear from ~60,000km (cold-start rattle) plus reports of elevated oil consumption. At 167,000km this listing is well past the mileage where both issues typically surface, so a pre-purchase inspection of the gearbox and engine (chain noise, oil level history) is important. The model overall scores well in aggregate reliability surveys (What Car? placed the current-gen 5008 3rd of 12 in its 7-seat class, ~95%), and start-stop glitches are a known but minor nuisance rather than a major fault. Evidence is a mix of consistent mechanic/parts-site write-ups and forum owner reports, with some owners reporting no issues at all, hence medium rather than high confidence. Sources: Peugeot Forums, AUTODOC, BreakerYard, What Car? (whatcar.com), PeugeotClub.eu.

reliability_summary: Kia Picanto (3rd-gen, 2020) with the 1.2L 84hp engine and 4-speed torque-converter automatic rates well overall: it placed 2nd of 20 in the What Car? 2024 small-car reliability survey (99.3%) and the 1.2L Kappa engine has a long, solid track record. The A4CF 4-speed automatic has scattered owner reports of shift flare or failing to smoothly engage 4th gear, but is generally described as trouble-free; a separate, unrelated 2020-2022 recall covered an instrument-cluster software chime fix, not the drivetrain. A known minor issue is a fuel-filler rubber hose that can crack and cause a fuel smell, a cheap fix. Some Hebrew-language sources mention a jerky 'robotic' AMT gearbox on Picanto, but that applies to the smaller 1.0L trim, not this 1.2/84hp variant, so it's noted as a possible source of confusion rather than a real risk here. Confidence is medium: survey data is strong and consistent, but detailed Israel-specific owner feedback on this exact 1.2 automatic combo is thin.

reliability_summary: Mixed verdict: the 6.6L gasoline V8 (GM's Israel-market replacement for the older 2.8L turbodiesel) shares its architecture with GM's Vortec/L8T small-block family, which US owner data rates as fundamentally reliable with only manageable issues (knock sensor corrosion, exhaust manifold bolts, water pump, minor oil consumption). The paired 8-speed automatic (8L90-family) has documented, more serious complaints: torque converter shudder, harsh/jerky shifts, clutch pack wear producing metal contamination, and a US class-action lawsuit over shudder/hesitation across ~800k GM 8-speed-equipped vehicles. NHTSA's 2023-2025 Express/Savana transmission investigation concerned the different 6L90 6-speed on cutaway models, not this van's 8-speed, so it doesn't directly apply here. This specific listing already had its engine replaced by the importer ~6 months ago at roughly 350,000 km, which both removes near-term engine risk and signals the original unit didn't reach that mileage cleanly. Israel-specific data on this gasoline-converted Savana is thin (mostly ads/test-drive puff pieces, no dedicated reliability survey), and a functioning parts/engine-swap market (motor-center.co.il) confirms replacements aren't rare for this model. Sources: chevytrucks.org, chevroletforum.com, slashgear.com/circledtrans.com (8L90), gmauthority.com/carscoops.com (NHTSA), queenoftheroad.co.il (Israel engine-swap context).

reliability_summary: Below-average reliability for this powertrain: the 2010 Superb's 1.8 TSI is an early EA888 Gen1 engine with a well-documented timing chain tensioner design flaw (ratchet mechanism failures reported at 40-80k miles) that can cause catastrophic engine damage if the chain jumps. Paired DSG (dry-clutch DQ200/similar) shows recurring mechatronic unit and clutch-shudder issues, with jerky 1st-2nd shifts common by 50-100k km. Israeli forum reports (FXP) add owner complaints of high oil consumption, a clutch replaced 3 times by 90,000 km, and turbo pipe failures around 80,000 km. Seller claims the engine and gearbox were replaced 8 years ago with only 60,000 km since - if true this mitigates risk, but it is unverified and the car is otherwise at 165,000 km, well past where these known faults typically appear. Sources are consistent across UK/int'l reviews, dedicated DSG repair shops, and Israeli owner forums, giving medium confidence; no independent survey data (JD Power/TÜV) specific to this generation was found.

reliability_summary: Mixed: the Allison 6-speed automatic is proven and durable (millions of miles in service, only high-mileage clutch/converter wear), but the paired 6.6L Duramax LML diesel (397hp, 2011-2016) has a well-documented design flaw in its Bosch CP4.2 high-pressure fuel pump, which fails from fuel-lubrication starvation and showers the fuel system with metal, typically costing $8,000-12,000+ to fully repair; failures can occur anywhere from 50k-150k+ miles with no warning. The LML's SCR/DEF emissions hardware (NOx sensors, DEF pump/heater) is also failure-prone with age. CarComplaints/NHTSA data for this model year is moderate (160 complaints across the 2013 Silverado 2500HD, engine and fuel system among the worst categories), and general US consensus rates the LML era as reliable at the block level but risky at the fuel system. Israeli-market data is thin: this generation Silverado was never officially imported (only the newer EV is), so it's a private/grey import in Israel with limited specialized service and parts availability, adding real risk to a high-mileage (285k km) diesel exposed to local fuel quality. Given the known CP4 design flaw on a car already at 285k km/40k, capping the score at 5 per the reliability rubric; confidence is medium since US sourcing is solid but Israel-specific data is sparse.
